title: My philosophy regarding upper back training (part. 1)
summary: His upper back philosophy: it tolerates the most volume, recovers fastest, and should be trained the most, ideally every day. Bodyweight pull-ups with rotating grips form the bulk of his volume, plus rows of all kinds, dumbbell pullovers for lats and dedicated shrugs for traps, with intensity varied across his 8-day program.

claims.claim: The upper back can take the most volume, recovers the fastest, and should be trained the most of any body part.
Because the upper back has so many muscles, you need objectivity and mind-muscle connection to know what you're really targeting; with imperfect form, stronger muscles take the work.
He trains his upper back in some way every training day, six days a week, varying intensity and volume.
Pull-ups should be the staple of everyone's program; bodyweight pull-ups can be done every day with no recovery issues and give great hypertrophy if you switch grips.
Sticking to one pull-up grip risks tendon and ligament overuse; rotating grips avoids it, and you won't get a lat or rhomboid injury from bodyweight pull-ups.
He likes all rows (chest-supported, dumbbell, barbell, rings); find a variation that hits the upper back, and if you feel it all in arms and shoulders you're doing it wrong or picked the wrong row.
Dumbbell pullovers give unmatched lat isolation and stretch.
He used to rely on deadlifts and floor pulls for traps but found it wasn't enough, so for about a year he has done dedicated trap isolation, especially shrugs.
His upper back lacks width partly from genetics and partly from not training lats smartly for a long time.
Pull-ups done with slow negatives are excellent for the lats.
On deadlift days he emphasises traps; on arm days lats and rear delts; two of eight program days deload the upper back with just a few pull-ups or hangs for a stretch.
In his 8-day program: two high-intensity deadlift days, two medium-intensity arm days, one high-intensity bench day and one high-intensity squat day for the upper back; the rest low or none.
Training the upper back once a week in a split is wrong, and even three full-body sessions a week misses upper back gains.
A strong upper back prevents a slouched-forward posture and shoulder impingement.
He wants a big, thick upper back because he has a wide waist; a beefy back draws the eye away from the waist when he turns around.

exercises.name: Bodyweight pull-ups
exercises.why: bulk of upper back volume, daily without recovery issues

exercises.name: Rows (chest-supported, dumbbell, barbell, rings)
